new_statements.quote: Stress is a word-level phenomenon in Nama in which a particular syllable has prominence or emphasis. It is not predictable, but the clear tendency is that the penultimate syllable is given primary stress. This means that in words of two syllables, the initial syllable is stressed. Lexical items are rarely longer than three syllables, with four the maximum, except for those with complete reduplication. [...] Exceptions in two syllable words include /wə.ˈrær/ wè.ˈrár ‘wallaby’ and /də.ˈɡin/ dè.ˈgin ‘fish type’. These are most often words in which the first syllable is open and the nucleus is /ə/. [...] Also, in reduplicated forms, each element retains the same stress as it would have individually
new_statements.citation: Siegel, Jeff. 2023. A Grammar of Nama: A Papuan Language of Southern New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics 668. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.4.3 Stress (p. 46) and Table 2.21 (p. 47). Print ISBN 978-3-11-107661-4; e-ISBN 978-3-11-107701-7.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statements for nama1266; this is the first primary-source statement (the language's reference grammar, by the fieldworker). It is consistent with the only related note already in for this glottocode, Kashima 2020 on the sister language Nmbo ('tends to fall on the penultimate syllable'), and with Evans 2021's regional remark that Southern New Guinea languages lack tone/distinctive stress only in the loose sense (Siegel shows a handful of lexical exceptions but no minimal stress pairs).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress exists and primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable as the clear default (2-syll: initial; 3-syll: medial; 4-5-syll incl. inflected forms: penult, e.g. /̩jən.kə.ma.ˈŋɡər.mən/ 'we slept'). The author states placement is 'not predictable' in the strict sense because a minority of lexical items deviate: some disyllables have final stress (mostly when the first syllable is open with a schwa nucleus, e.g. wè.ˈrár 'wallaby'), some trisyllables have initial stress (ˈga.si.yè 'crocodile', ˈsá.lá.me 'clothes') or final stress (mè.ngo.ˈtu 'village', a.ra.ˈkaf 'sea'). In full reduplications each copy keeps its own stress (ˈfè.rèn-ˈfè.rèn). No tone; acute/grave accents in the orthography mark vowel quality (á=/æ/, è=/ə/), not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in prose, but the transcriptions in Table 2.21 and the exceptions mark a secondary stress (low vertical stroke) on the word-initial syllable of 4- and 5-syllable words (/̩æ.ɸi.ˈtræ.rəɣ/ 'come off', /̩ɸə.jo.ta.ˈoɸ.nar/ 'unfair', /̩jən.kə.ma.ˈŋɡər.mən/ 'we slept') and of final-stressed trisyllables (/̩mə.ŋɡo.ˈtu/ 'village', /̩a.ra.ˈkaɸ/ 'sea').
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables with final stress, 'most often words in which the first syllable is open and the nucleus is /ə/' (wè.ˈrár 'wallaby', dè.ˈgin 'fish type'); trisyllables with initial stress (ˈga.si.yè 'crocodile', ˈsá.lá.me 'clothes') or final stress (mè.ngo.ˈtu 'village', a.ra.ˈkaf 'sea'); reduplicated forms keep the stress of each element (ˈfè.rèn-ˈfè.rèn 'pattern', gi.ˈdá.min-gi.ˈdá.min 'plant type'). Elsewhere (§2.2, p. ~40) [ɪ] is noted as an allophone of /ə/ 'normally in unstressed syllables'.
new_statements.identity_note: Siegel 2023 describes Nama [ˈnəmə], ISO 639-3 nmx, Nambu subgroup of the Yam (formerly Morehead-Upper Maro) family, c. 1200 speakers in Daraia, Mata and Ngaraita villages near Morehead, South Fly District, Western Province, PNG; the grammar focuses on the Mata/Daraia dialect (the Ngaraita dialect differs only in a few lexical items, Appendix A). This is the Papuan Nama of glottocode nama1266, not Khoekhoe (Nama) of Namibia.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas. 2021. The phonetics of Papuan languages in Southern New Guinea: an overview. In K. Lindsey & D. Schokkin (eds), Phonetic fieldwork in Southern New Guinea (Language Documentation & Conservation Special Publication 24). Honolulu: UH Press. (ANU Open Research hdl:1885/291011).
sources.note: Regional generalisation only (p. 7): 'it is difficult to identify any typological features of the phonologies of Southern New Guinea, other than absences (e.g., no tone, no pitch accent or distinctive stress except for Urama, no ejectives etc.)'. Nama is not treated individually.

sources.citation: Kashima, Eri. 2020. Language In My Mouth: Linguistic Variation in the Nmbo Speech Community of Southern New Guinea. PhD thesis, Australian National University. hdl:1885/201927.
sources.note: About the sister language Nmbo only (p. 109): 'Nmbo stress is obligatory, and tends to fall on the penultimate syllable.' Cites Siegel's Nama work for morphology; says nothing about Nama stress.

sources.note: Nothing. Only an orthography footnote (fn. 1: <è> = /ə/, <á> = /æ/, <ú> = /y/, <ó> = /ø/ — the acute marks vowel quality, not stress) and remarks on schwa epenthesis/syncope; no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent'.
